prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) -- Heavy rains smashed through a dam near Indonesia's capital Friday, unleashing a torrent of water that plowed into hundreds of homes and killed at least 52 people in what some survivors described as a suburban "tsunami." Members of a search and rescue team look for bodies around upended trees and vehicles near  Jakarta Friday. Sleeping residents were taken by surprise by the powerful flash flood as it crashed through Jakarta's crowded Cirendeu suburb, in the early hours of the morning. Rescue crews suspended their search for survivors overnight Friday evening, the National Disaster Coordination Agency said. The agency put the death toll at 52 with 17 missing. It said 33 people were injured and 1,490 left homeless. The Indonesian Health Ministry put the death toll higher at 58 people. After the deluge, drenched, injured and shivering survivors took refuge on the rooftops of their homes as rescuers in rubber boats struggled to reach them. Social affairs spokesman official Mardjito, who like many Indonesians goes by one name, said relief efforts were being hampered by debris from the dam. "We're still trying to get into the houses, but the problem is, mud is getting in our way," he said. Pictures from the scene showed the pulverized ruins of wooden buildings emerging as brown muddied waters subside.  Watch scenes of the flood devastation » . Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, currently on the campaign trail ahead of elections later this year, said he had ordered senior ministers to visit the scene of the disaster. "On behalf of the government, I express my condolences to the families of the dead victims and may their souls be accepted by God almighty," he said, according to the official Antara news agency. The rain obliterated a 255-meter-long section of the dam at around 4 am local time, releasing a wall of water from the 20-hectare lake that some survivors said reminded them of the tsunami that hit Indonesia in 2004. "They said they had heard loud rumbling sounds like during a powerful earthquake. They later found out that the sounds came from the water rushing out from the dam's lake," Antara said. Survivors told stories of dead relatives and harrowing brushes with death as they struggled to escape rising waters. Dewi Masitoh, a 40-year-old housewife, told the AFP news agency that she escaped with her husband and two daughters after they saw rising water reach the door of their stilt house. "We were on the second floor but my daughter went back downstairs when the window broke and water gushed in. My husband jumped in and pulled her out of the water by her neck. "I punched a hole through the roof and we all climbed up through," she said, showing cuts and scratches on her arms." Floods from heavy rains are an annual occurrence around Jakarta, a low lying city on the northern coast of Java island, where poor infrastructure often results in polluted canals and rivers spilling their banks and spilling into thousands of homes. In 2007, 38 people were killed and 430,000 forced from their homes when storm waters three meters deep in some places swamped 75 percent of the capital, which is home to about 9 million people. With poor sanitation and a hot and humid climate, the risk of water-borne diseases is usually a major concern following floods in the city, where mosquito-transmitted malaria is also a threat. CNN's Andy Saputra contributed to this report.

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) — Torrential rain breached a dam near the Indonesian capital early Friday, sending a massive surge of water through hundreds of houses and leaving at least 52 people dead. Some survivors compared the disaster to a “tsunami” striking the suburbs.

Search-and-rescue personnel combed an area near Jakarta littered with overturned vehicles and uprooted trees as they looked for bodies. The flash flood swept into the densely populated Cirendeu suburb before dawn, catching residents asleep and unprepared.

The National Disaster Coordination Agency said rescue teams halted their search overnight on Friday. According to the agency, 52 people had died, 17 remained missing, 33 were injured and 1,490 had been displaced. Indonesia’s Health Ministry reported a higher fatality count of 58.

In the flood’s aftermath, soaked, wounded and trembling residents gathered on rooftops while rescuers in inflatable boats struggled to reach them. Mardjito, a social affairs official who, like many Indonesians, uses a single name, said wreckage from the dam was obstructing relief operations. He explained that crews were still attempting to enter homes but were being slowed by thick mud.

Images from the disaster zone showed the shattered remains of wooden structures becoming visible as the muddy brown water receded.

President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, who was campaigning ahead of elections scheduled for later that year, said he had instructed senior government ministers to travel to the affected area. In remarks carried by the state-run Antara news agency, he offered the government’s sympathy to the victims’ families and prayed that the dead would be received by God Almighty.

At approximately 4 a.m. local time, the rainfall destroyed a 255-meter stretch of the dam, releasing a wall of water from a 20-hectare lake. Several survivors said the experience recalled the tsunami that devastated Indonesia in 2004.

Antara reported that residents initially heard a powerful roaring noise resembling the sound of a major earthquake. They later realized it had been caused by water surging out of the dam’s reservoir.

Survivors recounted losing relatives and narrowly escaping death as the water rapidly rose. Dewi Masitoh, a 40-year-old homemaker, told Agence France-Presse that she, her husband and their two daughters fled after the water climbed to the entrance of their elevated house.

Masitoh said the family had reached the second floor, but one daughter returned downstairs just as a window shattered and water rushed inside. Her husband jumped into the flood and pulled the girl out by the neck. Masitoh then broke through the roof so the entire family could climb to safety. As she told the story, cuts and scratches were visible on her arms.

Flooding caused by seasonal downpours occurs every year in and around Jakarta. The capital sits on low-lying ground along the northern coast of Java, and inadequate infrastructure frequently allows contaminated rivers and canals to overflow into thousands of residences.

In 2007, floodwater reaching three meters in some locations covered 75 percent of the city, killing 38 people and forcing 430,000 from their homes. Jakarta has a population of roughly 9 million.

Because of poor sanitation and the city’s hot, humid conditions, flooding typically raises serious fears of waterborne illness. Malaria, which is spread by mosquitoes, is another danger.

CNN’s Andy Saputra contributed to the report.

counterfactuals.output:
# BREAKING NEWS: Dam collapse unleashes deadly flooding near Jakarta

**TANGERANG, Indonesia** — A dam holding back the Situ Gintung reservoir burst after torrential rain, sending a wall of water through a densely populated neighborhood southwest of Jakarta and killing about 100 people, Indonesian authorities said.

The collapse occurred before dawn on March 27, 2009, while many residents were asleep. The surge swept away homes, overturned vehicles and left streets buried beneath mud, timber and concrete. Casualty figures varied as rescue teams searched the devastated area, with officials reporting roughly 100 deaths and dozens of people initially missing. Hundreds of residents were displaced.

Survivors described being jolted awake by a thunderous sound before water rushed into their homes. Some said they escaped by climbing onto rooftops or trees, while others were carried hundreds of yards by the current. Families gathered near the wreckage, searching lists of survivors and waiting for news of missing relatives.

Soldiers, police officers, emergency workers and volunteers dug through thick mud and piles of debris, using heavy machinery where possible. Rescue operations were complicated by blocked roads, unstable structures and continuing rain. Temporary shelters were established in schools, government buildings and other public facilities, where displaced residents received food, water and medical care.

Officials said intense rainfall caused the reservoir to overflow and breach part of its aging earthen embankment. Investigators were ordered to determine whether poor maintenance or structural weaknesses contributed to the disaster.

Then-President **Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono** visited the flood zone, expressed condolences to victims’ families and promised government assistance and a full investigation. Local authorities also faced questions from residents who said they had previously raised concerns about the condition of the dam.

The Situ Gintung disaster became one of the deadliest dam failures in modern Indonesian history, highlighting the risks posed by aging infrastructure and rapid urban development around Jakarta.

counterfactuals.output:
**“Suburban tsunami” devastates Jakarta neighborhood after Situ Gintung dam bursts**

**CIRENDEU, Indonesia, March 2009** — A torrent of water unleashed by the collapse of the Situ Gintung reservoir embankment swept through a densely populated suburb southwest of Jakarta before dawn, killing about 100 people, destroying hundreds of homes and forcing large numbers of residents into emergency shelters.

The disaster struck in the early hours of March 27 after heavy rain swelled the Dutch colonial-era reservoir in Cirendeu, part of the Ciputat area of Tangerang, on the outskirts of the Indonesian capital. As the earthen dam gave way, water, mud, trees and debris surged downhill into sleeping neighborhoods.

Survivors described a sudden roar followed by a wall of water several meters high. The force of the flood tore houses from their foundations, overturned vehicles and carried residents through narrow streets. Indonesian media quickly called the disaster a **“suburban tsunami,”** a phrase that captured both the speed of the inundation and the devastation left behind.

By the end of rescue operations, authorities reported roughly 100 confirmed deaths, although totals varied as officials reconciled hospital, police and missing-person records. Some victims were found kilometers from their homes, buried beneath mud or trapped in the wreckage of buildings. Search teams continued to look for missing residents in piles of timber, roofing, furniture and household debris.

Hundreds of houses were destroyed or badly damaged. In the hardest-hit areas, little remained beyond broken concrete walls and tangled electrical cables. Roads became channels of thick mud, complicating the movement of ambulances and heavy equipment. The flood also damaged public facilities and inundated nearby educational and community buildings.

Hundreds of survivors were displaced, with some estimates placing the number of people temporarily driven from their homes at more than 1,000. Many took refuge in schools, mosques, government buildings and makeshift tents. Relief agencies and volunteers distributed bottled water, cooked food, blankets, clothing and medicine, while officials worked to identify the dead and reunite separated families.

Health workers warned that the emergency could produce a second crisis. Floodwater had mixed with sewage, garbage and mud, contaminating wells and other local water sources. Crowded shelters, limited sanitation and shortages of clean water increased the threat of diarrhea, skin infections and respiratory illness. Children and older residents were considered especially vulnerable.

The presence of human and animal remains in the affected area added to public anxiety. Health specialists stressed that decomposing bodies generally pose less risk of epidemic disease than contaminated drinking water, but urged their rapid recovery and dignified handling. Authorities also monitored for mosquito-borne illnesses as pools of stagnant water formed around damaged homes.

Attention soon turned to the condition and management of the reservoir. Situ Gintung had been built during Dutch colonial rule and later became a recreational lake surrounded by expanding residential development. Residents said they had noticed erosion, leaks or other warning signs before the collapse, prompting questions about whether the embankment had been properly inspected and maintained.

Officials said intense rainfall had caused the reservoir to overflow and weaken the structure. Investigators examined whether a spillway or drainage channel had failed to release water quickly enough and whether years of settlement around the lake had increased the scale of the disaster.

President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono visited the area and ordered emergency assistance for survivors. The government faced pressure to provide compensation, rebuild homes and inspect other aging dams and reservoirs in and around Jakarta.

For Cirendeu residents, however, the immediate task was recovering relatives and possessions from the mud. Families gathered at hospitals and temporary morgues, while survivors returned cautiously to the wrecked neighborhood to search for identification papers, photographs and anything else the water had left behind.

The Situ Gintung disaster became one of the deadliest dam failures in modern Indonesian history and a stark warning about the risks created when aging water infrastructure, extreme rainfall and dense urban development converge.

counterfactuals.output:
## Situ Gintung dam disaster, Indonesia

In the early hours of **27 March 2009**, part of the embankment holding back **Situ Gintung**, a roughly **20-hectare artificial lake** southwest of Jakarta, collapsed after heavy rain. A wall of water swept through the densely populated Cirendeu area of Tangerang, destroying or badly damaging hundreds of homes.

Contemporary casualty figures changed as rescue operations continued, but reports put the toll at **about 100 dead**, with **roughly 100 people missing** and **more than 150 injured**. Several hundred residents were left homeless and sheltered in temporary evacuation centers.

President **Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono** visited the disaster area, met survivors, and directed government agencies to accelerate rescue and relief work. He promised assistance and compensation for affected families, ordered an investigation into the cause of the breach, and called for inspections of other aging dams and reservoirs.

The disaster was smaller in geographic scale than **Jakarta’s February 2007 floods**, which inundated large parts of the capital, killed **more than 50 people**, and forced approximately **400,000–500,000 residents** from their homes. Nevertheless, the Situ Gintung collapse was especially destructive locally because the water was released suddenly into neighborhoods immediately below the embankment.
